title: 1  The Basic Idea of RL, and Its Link to Dynamic Programming
text:
1.1 The basic idea of RL
This chapter follows Ben Moll’s Lecture 1. Reinforcement learning is Monte-Carlo dynamic programming: it uses Bellman recursions with expectations estimated from samples rather than computed from a known model.
For a random variable \(x\), compute \(\E[x]\) by integration or sampling:
The Monte-Carlo mean can be built up incrementally. Writing \(\bar{x}_{k}=\tfrac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}\) for the running mean of the first \(k\) samples, the recursion is
\[
\bar{x}_{k}=\bar{x}_{k-1}+\frac{1}{k}\,(x_{k}-\bar{x}_{k-1}).
\tag{1.1}\]

text:
Exact. If we know the distribution \(p(x)\), integrate: \[
\E[x]=\int x\,p(x)\,dx .
\]
Monte Carlo. If we do not know \(p(x)\) but can sample \(\vec{x}=[x_{1},\dots,x_{N}]'\), average: \[
\E[x]\approx \bar{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i} .
\]









Tip



The step size \(\tfrac{1}{k}\) is the learning rate. A constant \(\alpha\) gives more weight to recent samples.



Computing a value function

Definition 1.1 (Markov reward process) A Markov reward process (MRP) assigns to each starting state \(s_{0}\) the discounted expected reward \[
v(s_{0})=\E\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}r(s_{t})\right],
\] where the state \(s_{t}\) follows an exogenous Markov process and \(\beta\in(0,1)\) is the discount factor.

For \(v\), the corresponding methods are:

Dynamic programming. If we know the transition density \(p(s'\given s)\), then \(v\) solves the fixed point \[
v(s)=r(s)+\beta\int v(s')\,p(s'\given s)\,ds' .
\tag{1.2}\]
Monte Carlo. If we cannot evaluate \(p\) but can sample trajectories \(\{s_{t}^{i}\}_{t=0}^{T}\), average the realized returns: \[
v(s_{0})\approx \hat{v}(s_{0})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=0}^{T}\beta^{t}r(s_{t}^{i}).
\]

Averaging whole trajectories requires waiting for each trajectory to finish. We can instead update \(\hat{v}\) at every step \(t\) of every trajectory \(k\), using the incremental rule Equation 1.1 with a constant learning rate \(\alpha\):
\[
\hat{v}_{t+1}^{k}(s_{t}^{k})=\hat{v}_{t}^{k}(s_{t}^{k})+\alpha\big[\,r(s_{t}^{k})+\beta\,\hat{v}_{t}^{k}(s_{t+1}^{k})-\hat{v}_{t}^{k}(s_{t}^{k})\,\big].
\tag{1.3}\]
This is the TD(0) update.






NoteDerivation: from the incremental mean to TD(0)





Start from the dynamic-programming fixed point Equation 1.2 and read it as an expectation: \[
v(s)=r(s)+\beta\int v(s')\,p(s'\given s)\,ds'
     =\E_{s'\sim p(\cdot\given s)}\big[\,\underbrace{r(s)+\beta v(s')}_{Y\,\defeq\,r(s)+\beta v(s')}\,\big].
\] Apply Equation 1.1 to \(\E[Y]\), using a constant learning rate \(\alpha\).
At trajectory \(k\) the realized value of \(Y\) is \(r(s^{k})+\beta v(s'^{k})\). The true \(v(s'^{k})\) is unknown. We bootstrap by substituting the current estimate \(\hat{v}^{k}\) in its place: \[
x_{k}=r(s^{k})+\beta\,\hat{v}^{k}(s'^{k}).
\] If \(\hat v^k\) converges uniformly to \(v\), the conditional bias of this target tends to zero. Feeding \(x_{k}\) into the incremental rule \(\bar{x}_{k}=\bar{x}_{k-1}+\alpha(x_{k}-\bar{x}_{k-1})\), with \(\bar{x}_{k}=\hat{v}'^{k}(s^{k})\) the updated estimate and \(\bar{x}_{k-1}=\hat{v}^{k}(s^{k})\) the old one (a prime marks the post-update value), gives \[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{v}'^{k}(s^{k})
  &=\hat{v}^{k}(s^{k})+\alpha\big[\,r(s^{k})+\beta\,\hat{v}^{k}(s'^{k})-\hat{v}^{k}(s^{k})\,\big] \\
  &=(1-\alpha)\,\hat{v}^{k}(s^{k})+\alpha\big[\,r(s^{k})+\beta\,\hat{v}^{k}(s'^{k})\,\big],
\end{aligned}
\] which is Equation 1.3 written one step at a time.









Tip



The bracketed quantity \(r+\beta\hat{v}(s')-\hat{v}(s)\) is the temporal-difference error, the gap between the one-step target and the current estimate.








NoteWhy a constant step size?



The step \(\tfrac{1}{k}\) in Equation 1.1 weights samples equally; for iid observations with finite variance, its variance falls like \(1/k\). The TD target \(r+\beta\,\hat{v}(s')\) moves as \(\hat{v}\) and the policy change, so shrinking steps can track it slowly.
A constant \(\alpha\) keeps weight on new observations. For iid targets with variance \(\sigma^2\) and \(0<\alpha<1\), the recursion \(\hat{v}\leftarrow(1-\alpha)\hat{v}+\alpha\cdot(\text{target})\) has limiting variance \(\alpha\sigma^2/(2-\alpha)\). Persistent noise leaves fluctuations; a deterministic contraction can converge with a constant step. The Robbins-Monro conditions below give sufficient conditions for convergence with noisy updates.


The trajectory average and the TD(0) update estimate the same \(v\) with different bias, variance and timing:



Table 1.1: Monte Carlo vs. TD(0) as estimators of the value function.

The two are endpoints of a spectrum: \(n\)-step returns and TD(\(\lambda\)) interpolate between them.







Figure 1.1: Both estimators use the same episodes from a five-state discounted Markov reward process; error is measured across all states. TD(0) has lower error at small budgets, then reaches a noise floor set by \(\alpha\). Monte Carlo eventually crosses below it.





Reinforcement learning and deep learning
Often we approximate the value function by a parametric family \[
\hat{V}(s,w),
\] where \(w\) is a parameter vector, for instance the weights of a neural network. Using a neural network gives deep reinforcement learning.






Note



RL estimates values and policies from sampled experience. A neural network is one choice of function approximator.

text:
1.2 Link to Dynamic Programming

Bellman equation with finite states

Definition 1.2 (Markov decision process) A stochastic optimal-control problem (or MDP) chooses controls to maximize discounted expected reward, \[
v(s_{0})=\max_{\{a_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}}\E_{0}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right]
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad s_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot\given s_{t},a_{t}),\ \ s_{0}\text{ given},
\] with state \(s\in\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{n}\}\) and control \(a\in\mathcal{A}\). The goal is an optimal policy \(a=\pi(s)\).


Example 1.1 (Neoclassical growth model) Force capital onto a finite grid \(\mathcal{K}=\{k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\}\) and solve \[
v(k_{0})=\max_{\{c_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}}\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}u(c_{t})
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad k_{t+1}=f(k_{t})+(1-\delta)k_{t}-c_{t}\in\mathcal{K}.
\] The dynamics are deterministic, so the transition “probabilities” are degenerate: \[
p(s'\given s,a)=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } s'=f(s)+(1-\delta)s-a \ \text{ and }\ s'\in\mathcal{K},\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

The value function satisfies the Bellman equation \[
v(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Big\{\,r(s,a)+\beta\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}v(s')\,p(s'\given s,a)\,\Big\}.
\tag{1.4}\]
Naming the bracketed quantity gives the action-value (or Q) function: \[
v(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Big\{\,\underbrace{r(s,a)+\beta\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}v(s')\,p(s'\given s,a)}_{\defeq\,q(s,a)}\,\Big\}=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q(s,a).
\]

Definition 1.3 (Action-value (Q) function) \(q(s,a)\) is the value of taking action \(a\) in state \(s\) and following the optimal policy \(\pi^{*}\) thereafter: \[
\begin{aligned}
\pi(s) &=\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q(s,a),\\[2pt]
q(s,a) &=r(s,a)+\E_{\pi^{*}}\!\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{\infty}\beta^{\tau}r(s_{t+\tau},a_{t+\tau})\ \given\ s_{t}=s,\,a_{t}=a\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

Definition 1.3 defines the optimal action-value \(q^{*}\): it assumes the optimal policy \(\pi^{*}\) is followed after the first action. Swapping \(\pi^{*}\) for an arbitrary policy \(\pi\) gives the policy-specific \(q_{\pi}\); the version under the current policy, \(q_{\pi_{k}}\), is what Howard policy iteration iterates on below.






NoteDerivation: the two forms of q(s,a) coincide





Start from \[
q(s,a)=r(s,a)+\beta\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}v(s')\,p(s'\given s,a),
\] and expand the continuation value, which by definition is itself an expectation taken from \(t+1\) onward: \[
v(s')=\E_{\pi^{*}}\!\left[\sum_{\tau=0}^{\infty}\beta^{\tau}r(s_{t+1+\tau},a_{t+1+\tau})\ \given\ s_{t+1}=s'\right].
\] Substitute and apply the law of total expectation, which collapses the sum over \(s'\) into a single conditional expectation: \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}v(s')\,p(s'\given s,a)
&=\E_{s_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot\given s,a)}\!\left[\E_{\pi^{*}}\!\left[\sum_{\tau=0}^{\infty}\beta^{\tau}r(s_{t+1+\tau},a_{t+1+\tau})\ \given\ s_{t+1}=s'\right]\right]\\
&=\E_{\pi^{*}}\!\left[\sum_{\tau=0}^{\infty}\beta^{\tau}r(s_{t+1+\tau},a_{t+1+\tau})\ \given\ s_{t}=s,\,a_{t}=a\right].
\end{aligned}
\] Reindex with \(k=\tau+1\): \[
\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}v(s')\,p(s'\given s,a)
=\E_{\pi^{*}}\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\beta^{k-1}r(s_{t+k},a_{t+k})\ \given\ s_{t}=s,\,a_{t}=a\right].
\] Finally, put this back and absorb the discount \(\beta\): \[
\begin{aligned}
q(s,a)
&=r(s,a)+\beta\,\E_{\pi^{*}}\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\beta^{k-1}r(s_{t+k},a_{t+k})\ \given\ s_{t}=s,\,a_{t}=a\right]\\
&=r(s,a)+\E_{\pi^{*}}\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\beta^{k}r(s_{t+k},a_{t+k})\ \given\ s_{t}=s,\,a_{t}=a\right],
\end{aligned}
\] which is exactly the discounted-sum form in Definition 1.3.





Matrix-vector form of the Bellman equation
Index the states \(s_{i},\ i=1,\dots,n\), and write \(r_{a}(s)=r(s,a)\) and \(p_{a}(s'\given s)=p(s'\given s,a)\). Then Equation 1.4 reads \[
v(s_{i})=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Big\{\,r_{a}(s_{i})+\beta\sum_{s_{j}\in\mathcal{S}}v(s_{j})\,p_{a}(s_{j}\given s_{i})\,\Big\}.
\] Stacking all states together yields the compact matrix-vector form \[
\mathbf{v}=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\big\{\,\mathbf{r}_{a}+\beta\,\mathbf{P}_{a}\mathbf{v}\,\big\},
\tag{1.5}\] where the maximization is component-wise, \[
\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}v(s_{1})\\ \vdots\\ v(s_{n})\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{r}_{a}=\begin{bmatrix}r_{a}(s_{1})\\ \vdots\\ r_{a}(s_{n})\end{bmatrix},
\] and \(\mathbf{P}_{a}\) is the \(n\times n\) transition matrix with entries \((\mathbf{P}_{a})_{ij}=p_{a}(s_{j}\given s_{i})\).


Value function iteration (VFI)
Iterate the Bellman operator Equation 1.5 to convergence, starting from any \(\mathbf{v}_{0}\): \[
\mathbf{v}_{k+1}=\max_{a}\big\{\,\mathbf{r}_{a}+\beta\,\mathbf{P}_{a}\mathbf{v}_{k}\,\big\}.
\]


Howard policy iteration (HPI)
Howard policy iteration alternates two steps until the policy stops changing. Given an initial policy \(\pi_{0}\):

Policy evaluation (PE) computes the value of following the current policy \(\pi_{k}\): \[
\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}=\mathbf{r}_{\pi_{k}}+\beta\,\mathbf{P}_{\pi_{k}}\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}.
\tag{1.6}\]
Policy improvement (PI) maximizes component-wise against that value: \[
\pi_{k+1}=\argmax_{\pi}\big\{\,\mathbf{r}_{\pi}+\beta\,\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}\,\big\}.
\]

HPI evaluates each policy exactly and often requires fewer iterations than VFI. With finitely many policies and strict improvement each round, it terminates in finitely many iterations (Figure 1.2).


Value function iteration and Howard policy iteration, and their error paths
def vfi(u, v0, iters):
    """Value function iteration: v_{j+1} = max_{k'} { u + beta v_j }."""
    v, path = v0.copy(), []
    for _ in range(iters):
        # The whole Bellman operator is this one line: `u + BETA * v[None, :]` forms
        # r_a + beta P_a v_k for every state-action pair at once, and the row-wise max
        # is the component-wise maximization. Infeasible k' carry u = -inf, so the max
        # is already a CONSTRAINED maximization.
        v = np.max(u + BETA * v[None, :], axis=1)
        path.append(v.copy())
    return np.array(path)


def hpi(u, v0, iters):
    """Howard policy iteration: greedy improvement, then EXACT policy evaluation.

    Starting from a value rather than a policy, the loop improves first and evaluates
    second, so iteration k returns v_{pi_{k+1}}.
    """
    v, path = v0.copy(), []
    for _ in range(iters):
        pol = np.argmax(u + BETA * v[None, :], axis=1)           # improvement
        # Assemble r_pi and P_pi from the greedy policy: under a deterministic policy
        # P_pi is a 0/1 selection matrix with one entry per row, which is what makes
        # the solve below cheap.
        r_pi = u[np.arange(NK), pol]
        P_pi = np.zeros((NK, NK))
        P_pi[np.arange(NK), pol] = 1.0
        # Exact evaluation: solve (I - beta P_pi) v_pi = r_pi outright rather than
        # iterating it. That solve is the Newton-like step in policy space.
        v = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(NK) - BETA * P_pi, r_pi)
        path.append(v.copy())
    return np.array(path)


u = ncgm_payoff()
v0 = np.zeros(NK)
v_star = vfi(u, v0, 2500)[-1]                                    # converged reference

n_v, n_h = 220, 24
err_v = np.max(np.abs(vfi(u, v0, n_v) - v_star), axis=1)
err_h = np.max(np.abs(hpi(u, v0, n_h) - v_star), axis=1)
floor = 1e-14
err_v, err_h = np.maximum(err_v, floor), np.maximum(err_h, floor)

fig, ax = new_ax(6.6, 4.4)
ax.semilogy(np.arange(1, n_v + 1), err_v, color=COL["sky"], lw=2.0, zorder=4)
ax.semilogy(
    np.arange(1, n_h + 1), err_h, color=COL["vermilion"], lw=2.2,
    marker="o", ms=4.5, zorder=5,
)

# the theoretical VFI rate: error falls by exactly beta each sweep
ax.semilogy(
    np.arange(1, n_v + 1), err_v[0] * BETA ** np.arange(n_v),
    color=GREY, lw=1.0, ls="--", zorder=2,
)

ax.set_xlim(0, 200)
ax.set_ylim(floor / 3, err_v[0] * 3)
ax.set_xlabel("iteration")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\|v_j - v^*\|_\infty$")
label_at(ax, 88, 3.0, "value function iteration", color=COL["sky"], fontsize=9.5)
label_at(ax, 88, 0.45, r"contracts at rate $\beta=0.96$, forever", color=GREY, fontsize=8.5)
label_at(ax, 28, 1e-13, "Howard policy iteration", color=COL["vermilion"], fontsize=9.5)
label_at(ax, 28, 2e-14, "policy stable at iteration 19", color=GREY, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_title("Neoclassical growth model: HPI terminates, VFI only decays")

# The figure's central claim, asserted rather than eyeballed: HPI really does reach
# VFI's fixed point, to machine precision, inside the 24 iterations plotted. If this
# ever stops holding, the book fails to render rather than shipping a false figure.
assert np.max(np.abs(hpi(u, v0, 20)[-1] - v_star)) < 1e-12, "HPI missed v*"

plt.show()








Figure 1.2: The two algorithms on the neoclassical growth model of Example 1.1, with capital discretised onto a 250-point grid and \(\beta=0.96\). VFI has contraction modulus \(\beta\); its log error path is nearly linear. HPI reaches machine precision at iteration 18, and the policy stops changing at iteration 19. Matching that accuracy by VFI takes on the order of \(\log(10^{-15})/\log\beta\approx850\) sweeps.











Important



The link to RL is to replace the exact policy-evaluation step Equation 1.6 with a Monte-Carlo estimate built from sampled trajectories, needing no knowledge of \(\mathbf{P}_{\pi_{k}}\).
With only the state value \(\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}\), the improvement step \(\argmax_{\pi}\{\mathbf{r}_{\pi}+\beta\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\mathbf{v}\}\) still reads off the model \((\mathbf{r},\mathbf{P})\) to turn a value into a decision. The fix is to estimate the action-value \(q_{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\) directly; improvement is then simply \(\pi(s)=\argmax_{a}q_{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\), a comparison of estimated \(q\)-values that needs no model. This use of \(q\) leads to Sarsa and Q-learning.


The evaluation step Equation 1.6 is a linear fixed point in \(\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}\), solvable two ways:

Closed form (one linear solve): \[
\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}=(I-\beta\,\mathbf{P}_{\pi_{k}})^{-1}\mathbf{r}_{\pi_{k}}.
\]
Iteratively (cheaper when \(n\) is large): \[
\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}^{\,j+1}=\mathbf{r}_{\pi_{k}}+\beta\,\mathbf{P}_{\pi_{k}}\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}^{\,j},\qquad j=0,1,2,\dots
\]

The improvement step is itself a Q-function maximization: \[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{k+1}(s)
&=\argmax_{\pi}\Big\{\,r(s,\pi)+\beta\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}v_{\pi_{k}}(s')\,p(s'\given s,\pi)\,\Big\}\\
&=\argmax_{\pi}q_{\pi_{k}}(s,\pi),
\end{aligned}
\] where \(q_{\pi_{k}}\) is the Q-function under policy \(\pi_{k}\). In vector form, \[
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{k+1}=\argmax_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\mathbf{q}_{\pi,\pi_{k}},
\qquad\text{with}\quad
\mathbf{q}_{a,\pi_{k}}=\mathbf{r}_{a}+\beta\,\mathbf{P}_{a}\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}.
\]

title: 2  Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Approximation
text:
2.1 Recall: the MDP in RL notation
Recall from Definition 1.2 the optimal control problem
\[
v(s_{0})=\max_{\{a_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}}\E_{0}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right]
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad s_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot\given s_{t},a_{t}),\ \ s_{0}\text{ given},
\]
whose solution is an optimal policy \(a=\pi(s)\). We now use two RL conventions.
Under a stochastic policy the maximization in the Bellman equation Equation 1.4 is over distributions over actions rather than over actions, so the one-step reward and the transition both get averaged against \(\pi\):
\[
v(s)=\max_{\pi}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\given s)
\left(r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p(s'\given s,a)\,v(s')\right).
\tag{2.1}\]
With Definition 2.1, Equation 2.1 collapses to the same shape as the deterministic case:
\[
v(s)=\max_{\pi}\left(r_{\pi}(s)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p_{\pi}(s'\given s)\,v(s')\right).
\tag{2.2}\]

NoteNotation: from β to γ, and from deterministic to stochastic policies



From this chapter onward:

the discount factor is written \(\gamma\) rather than \(\beta\);
policies are stochastic, \(a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\given s_{t})\), so \(\pi(a\given s)\) is a probability rather than a chosen action.






Definition 2.1 (Policy-averaged reward and transition) For a policy \(\pi\), define the policy-averaged reward and the policy-averaged transition \[
r_{\pi}(s)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\given s)\,r(s,a),
\qquad
p_{\pi}(s'\given s)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\given s)\,p(s'\given s,a).
\]









Tip



Fixing \(\pi\) gives an MRP (Definition 1.1) with reward \(r_{\pi}\) and transition \(p_{\pi}\). Chapter 1’s matrix equations apply with \(\mathbf{r}_{\pi}\) and \(\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\) from Definition 2.1.

title: 2  Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Approximation
text:
2.2 Monte Carlo methods

Where the model still hides
Recall the two steps of Howard policy iteration, now in RL notation:
\[
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}} &= \mathbf{r}_{\pi_{k}}+\gamma\,\mathbf{P}_{\pi_{k}}\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}} \\[2pt]
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{k+1} &= \argmax_{\pi}\big(\mathbf{r}_{\pi}+\gamma\,\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\mathbf{v}_{\pi_{k}}\big)
\end{cases}
\tag{2.3}\]
The first step is policy evaluation (PE), and the second is policy improvement (PI). State by state, PI is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{k+1}(s)
&=\argmax_{\pi}\sum_{a}\pi(a\given s)\Big[\underbrace{r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\given s,a)\,v_{\pi_{k}}(s')}_{\defeq\ q_{\pi_{k}}(s,a)}\Big]\\
&=\argmax_{\pi}\sum_{a}\pi(a\given s)\,q_{\pi_{k}}(s,a).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.4}\]


Two expressions for the action value
The action value of Definition 1.3 has a model-based and a return-based expression:
\[
q_{\pi_{k}}(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\given s,a)\,v_{\pi_{k}}(s')
\tag{2.5}\]
\[
q_{\pi_{k}}(s,a)=\E_{\pi_{k}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\ \given\ s_{0}=s,\,a_{0}=a\right]
\tag{2.6}\]



Table 2.1: The same action value, obtained from a model or from data.











Model-based form Equation 2.5
Model-free form Equation 2.6




Needs
the transition density \(p(s'\given s,a)\) and the reward \(r(s,a)\)
trajectories generated by \(\pi_{k}\)


Computed by
a sum over next states
an average over sampled returns


Available when
the model is known
you can only interact with the environment






The derivation under Definition 1.3 establishes their equivalence.


Estimating \(q\) from episodes

start from \((s,a)\), follow \(\pi_{k}\), and generate an episode \(t=0,1,\dots,T\);
do this \(N\) times, collecting episodes \(i=1,2,\dots,N\);
average the realized returns:

\[
q_{\pi_{k}}(s,a)
=\E_{\pi_{k}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\ \given\ s_{0}=s,\,a_{0}=a\right]
\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}r\big(s_{t}^{i},a_{t}^{i}\big).
\tag{2.7}\]






WarningSampling error and truncation bias



Equation 2.7 introduces two distinct sources of error:

a finite number of episodes \(N\), which is sampling error;
truncation at \(T\), which drops the continuation return. If \(|r|\le R\), its absolute expected size is at most \(R\gamma^{T+1}/(1-\gamma)\).

Increasing \(N\) averages out sampling noise; increasing \(T\) reduces the omitted tail.




Truncation bias in closed form, sampling error by simulation

for gamma, colour, y in ((0.90, COL["sky"], 8e-3), (0.99, COL["vermilion"], 2.0)):

    rewards = RNG.normal(rbar, sd, (reps, N, T_fix + 1))
    est = (rewards * disc).sum(axis=2).mean(axis=1)

Left: truncating each episode at \(T\) leaves a deterministic bias \(\gamma^{T+1}\bar{r}/(1-\gamma)\), geometric in \(T\) but with a rate set by \(\gamma\): at \(\gamma=0.9\) two hundred steps buys eight digits, at \(\gamma=0.99\) it buys barely one. Right: averaging \(N\) episodes leaves sampling error of order \(N^{-1/2}\) (dots simulated at \(\gamma=0.9\), \(T=200\); dashed line the \(-1/2\) reference slope), independent of \(\gamma\). Buying a digit of accuracy costs a fixed number of extra steps but a hundredfold increase in episodes.







The MC Basic algorithm
Substituting Equation 2.7 for the evaluation step of Equation 2.3 gives MC Basic.






NoteAlgorithm: MC Basic



Given an initial policy \(\pi_{0}\), at iteration \(k\), for every state \(s\in\mathcal{S}\) and every action \(a\in\mathcal{A}(s)\):

Collect sufficiently many episodes starting from \((s,a)\) and following \(\pi_{k}\).
Policy evaluation. Estimate the action value by the average return over those episodes: \[
q_{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\approx q_{k}(s,a)=\text{average return of all collected episodes}.
\]
Policy improvement. Act greedily with respect to the estimate: \[
a_{k}^{*}(s)=\argmax_{a}q_{k}(s,a),
\qquad
\pi_{k+1}(a\given s)=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } a=a_{k}^{*}(s),\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]






Table 2.2: MC Basic is Howard policy iteration with sample averages in place of the exact evaluation step.

Step 1 assumes episodes can be started from any pair \((s,a)\), an assumption usually called exploring starts. This supplies exploration; the next section replaces it with policy-based exploration.
With exact action values, the greedy step is ordinary policy improvement. Finite batches can reverse the ranking of two actions, even when both estimates are close. The policy-iteration convergence theorem applies in the exact-evaluation limit; a finite-sample convergence result also needs a schedule controlling these evaluation errors.






Important



MC Basic discards previous batches and collects fresh episodes for every state-action pair at every iteration, making it sample-inefficient.




Removing exploring starts: \(\eps\)-greedy policies
Exploring starts requires resetting the environment to an arbitrary state-action pair, which is usually unavailable. Greedy improvement in step 3 of MC Basic assigns probability 1 to one action, so following it supplies no data about other actions. A policy that retains some randomization supplies exploration without arbitrary resets.

Definition 2.2 (ε-greedy policy) For \(\eps\in[0,1]\), choose one maximizer of \(q(s,\cdot)\) using a fixed tie-breaking rule. The \(\eps\)-greedy policy is \[
\pi(a\given s)=
\begin{cases}
1-\dfrac{\eps}{|\mathcal{A}(s)|}\big(|\mathcal{A}(s)|-1\big) & \text{if } a=\argmax_{a'}q(s,a'),\\[8pt]
\dfrac{\eps}{|\mathcal{A}(s)|} & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]







Tip



With probability \(1-\eps\), choose the selected maximizer; with probability \(\eps\), draw uniformly from all actions. For \(\eps>0\), every action has probability at least \(\eps/|\mathcal A(s)|\). The endpoints are the greedy policy at \(\eps=0\) and the uniform policy at \(\eps=1\).


For a fixed policy with \(\eps>0\) on a finite continuing MDP, irreducibility of the induced state chain gives infinitely many visits to every state-action pair almost surely. Reachability from the starting state is insufficient: a chain that moves from state 0 to absorbing state 1 visits state 0 only once. In an episodic problem, visitation must come from repeated episodes and their reset distribution.






Warning



With exact \(q_\pi\), the \(\eps\)-greedy update is a policy-improvement step when \(\pi(a\mid s)\ge\eps/|\mathcal A(s)|\) for all pairs: it maximizes \(\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)q_\pi(s,a)\) subject to those same probability floors. Fixed \(\eps>0\) therefore restricts the policies available. Convergence to an unrestricted optimum requires both increasingly greedy policies and enough exploration to estimate every relevant action value; \(\eps_t\to0\) alone gives neither accurate estimates nor infinite visitation.

title: 2  Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Approximation
text:
2.3 Stochastic approximation

Motivating example: mean estimation
Given a random variable \(X\) and iid samples \(\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\), estimate \(\E[X]\) by
\[
\E[X]\approx\bar{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i},
\qquad
\lim_{N\to\infty}\bar{x}=\E[X].
\]
Let \(w_{k+1}\) denote the average of the first \(k\) samples,
\[
w_{k+1}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i},\qquad k=1,2,\dots
\]
so that \(w_{k}=\frac{1}{k-1}\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}x_{i}\). The incremental form is:






NoteDerivation: the incremental mean





\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{k+1}&=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}\\
&=\frac{1}{k}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}x_{i}+x_{k}\right)\\
&=\frac{1}{k}\big[(k-1)w_{k}+x_{k}\big]\\
&=w_{k}+\frac{1}{k}(x_{k}-w_{k}).
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\frac{1}{k}\,(w_{k}-x_{k}).
\tag{2.8}\]






NoteIndexing



Equation 2.8 is Equation 1.1 from Chapter 1 with the index shifted: here \(w_{k+1}\) is the mean of the first \(k\) samples, there \(\bar{x}_{k}\) is. The \(w\) convention matches the Robbins-Monro notation below.


Now generalize by replacing the step \(\tfrac{1}{k}\) with an arbitrary positive \(\alpha_{k}\):
\[
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}(w_{k}-x_{k}).
\tag{2.9}\]






NoteImplementation: the generalized incremental mean





In Equation 2.9, alpha is a constant or an array of steps \(\alpha_{k}\). With \(\alpha_{k}=1/k\), the estimate is the mean of the first \(k\) samples regardless of \(w_{0}\).

def mean_estimation_path(x, alpha, w0):
    """Run w_{k+1} = w_k - alpha_k (w_k - x_k) over the sample stream x.

    Returns the path [w_1, ..., w_{N+1}] of estimates.
    """
    n = len(x)
    a = np.full(n, alpha, float) if np.isscalar(alpha) else np.asarray(alpha, float)
    w = np.empty(n + 1)
    w[0] = w0
    for k in range(n):
        w[k + 1] = w[k] - a[k] * (w[k] - x[k])
    return w

x = np.random.default_rng(20260725).normal(0.0, 1.0, 50)
w = mean_estimation_path(x, 1.0 / np.arange(1, 51), w0=99.0)
assert np.allclose(w[1:], np.cumsum(x) / np.arange(1, 51))   # 1/k IS the running mean




Convergence to \(\E[X]\) follows from the Robbins-Monro conditions on \(\{\alpha_{k}\}\) below.


The Robbins-Monro algorithm
Stochastic approximation (SA) uses stochastic iterative algorithms for root-finding or optimization. It can operate with noisy function observations, without an explicit objective or its derivative. The Robbins-Monro (RM) algorithm is an early example; stochastic gradient descent is a special case, and its convergence theorem explains Equation 2.9.






NotePreliminary: the gradient



For a scalar function \(J(w)\) with \(w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{m})\in\R^{m}\), the gradient is the column vector \[
\nabla_{w}J(w)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\partial J(w)/\partial w_{1}\\
\partial J(w)/\partial w_{2}\\
\vdots\\
\partial J(w)/\partial w_{m}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]


Problem statement. Find the root of
\[
g(w)=0,
\]
where \(w\in\R\) is the variable to be solved for and \(g:\R\to\R\).






NoteOn dimension



The theorem and proof below are stated for scalar \(w\), because the proof’s mean value theorem step needs a single intermediate point and that is a one-dimensional fact. Everything survives in \(\R^{m}\) with two substitutions: replace the mean value theorem by the integral form \(g(w_{k})-g(w^{*})=\big[\int_{0}^{1}\nabla_{w}g\big(w^{*}+\tau\Delta_{k}\big)\,d\tau\big]\Delta_{k}\), and replace condition 1 by a uniform spectral bound \(0<c_{1}I\preceq\nabla_{w}g(w)\preceq c_{2}I\) on the Jacobian. The vector case is what Chapters 3 and 4 actually use, since there \(w\) and \(\theta\) are parameter vectors.








Tip



Optimization also leads to root-finding. If \(J(w)\) is an objective to be minimized, its first-order condition \(g(w)=\nabla_{w}J(w)=0\) is a root-finding problem.


The method for solving \(g(w)=0\) depends on the information available:

Model-based. If the expression of \(g\) is known, standard numerical algorithms apply.
Model-free. What if the expression of \(g\) is unknown, and all we obtain are noisy observations of its values?

RM solves the second case:
\[
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}\,\tilde{g}(w_{k},\eta_{k}),
\tag{2.10}\]
where \(w_{k}\) is the \(k\)-th estimate of the root, \(\tilde{g}(w_{k},\eta_{k})=g(w_{k})+\eta_{k}\) is the \(k\)-th noisy observation, and \(\alpha_{k}>0\) is the step size.

Theorem 2.1 (Robbins-Monro) In the RM algorithm Equation 2.10, suppose

\(0<c_{1}\leq\nabla_{w}g(w)\leq c_{2}\) for all \(w\);
\(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{k}=\infty\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{k}^{2}<\infty\);
\(\E[\eta_{k}\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]=0\) and \(\E[\eta_{k}^{2}\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]\leq C\) almost surely, for a constant \(C\) not depending on \(k\),

where \(\mathcal{H}_{k}=\{w_{k},w_{k-1},\dots\}\). Then \(w_{k}\) converges with probability 1 to the root \(w^{*}\) satisfying \(g(w^{*})=0\).







TipReading the three conditions




\(g\) is increasing and well-conditioned. The lower bound \(c_{1}>0\) makes the root unique and guarantees the update always points toward it; the upper bound \(c_{2}\) stops the steps from overshooting arbitrarily far.
The steps are large enough in total, small enough individually. \(\sum\alpha_{k}=\infty\) means the iteration can still travel an unbounded distance and so cannot stall short of the root no matter where it starts. \(\sum\alpha_{k}^{2}<\infty\) means \(\alpha_{k}\to0\) fast enough that the accumulated noise stays finite and the estimate settles. The canonical choice \(\alpha_{k}=1/k\) satisfies both, which is exactly the step in Equation 2.8.
The noise is zero-mean with finite variance. Unbiased observations, so errors cancel rather than accumulate into a drift.

A constant \(\alpha\) violates condition 2: \(\sum\alpha=\infty\) holds, but \(\sum\alpha^{2}=\infty\) too.




Why the Robbins-Monro theorem is true
Dvoretzky’s theorem proves Theorem 2.1 and also supports the convergence arguments in the next chapter.

Theorem 2.2 (Dvoretzky) Consider the stochastic process \[
\Delta_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_{k})\Delta_{k}+\beta_{k}\eta_{k},
\tag{2.11}\] where \(\{\alpha_{k}\},\{\beta_{k}\},\{\eta_{k}\}\) are stochastic sequences with \(\alpha_{k}\geq0\) and \(\beta_{k}\geq0\). Then \(\Delta_{k}\) converges to zero almost surely if

\(\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}=\infty\), \(\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}^{2}<\infty\), and \(\sum_{k}\beta_{k}^{2}<\infty\) uniformly almost surely;
\(\E[\eta_{k}\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]=0\) and \(\E[\eta_{k}^{2}\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]\leq C\) almost surely,

where \(\mathcal{H}_{k}=\{\Delta_{k},\Delta_{k-1},\dots,\eta_{k-1},\dots,\alpha_{k-1},\dots,\beta_{k-1},\dots\}\) is the history.







Tip



The steps \(\alpha_{k}\) and \(\beta_{k}\) may depend on the history, which allows the effective step size in the RM proof below. The conclusion is almost-sure convergence. The proof of Theorem 2.2 rests on quasimartingale convergence and is not reproduced here.








NoteProof of the Robbins-Monro theorem





Let \(w^{*}\) be the root, so \(g(w^{*})=0\), and write the RM algorithm Equation 2.10 with the noisy observation expanded: \[
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}\tilde{g}(w_{k},\eta_{k})=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}\big[g(w_{k})+\eta_{k}\big].
\] Subtract \(w^{*}\) from both sides and use \(g(w^{*})=0\): \[
w_{k+1}-w^{*}=w_{k}-w^{*}-\alpha_{k}\big[g(w_{k})-g(w^{*})+\eta_{k}\big].
\] By the mean value theorem there is a \(w_{k}'\) between \(w_{k}\) and \(w^{*}\) with \[
g(w_{k})-g(w^{*})=\nabla_{w}g(w_{k}')\,(w_{k}-w^{*}).
\] Writing \(\Delta_{k}\defeq w_{k}-w^{*}\) for the error and substituting, \[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{k+1}&=\Delta_{k}-\alpha_{k}\big[\nabla_{w}g(w_{k}')\Delta_{k}+\eta_{k}\big]\\
&=\Big[1-\underbrace{\alpha_{k}\nabla_{w}g(w_{k}')}_{\defeq\,\bar{\alpha}_{k}}\Big]\Delta_{k}+\underbrace{\alpha_{k}}_{\beta_{k}}(-\eta_{k}),
\end{aligned}
\] which is precisely Equation 2.11. It remains to check its two conditions.
Condition 1. By hypothesis 1 of Theorem 2.1, \(0<c_{1}\leq\nabla_{w}g(w)\leq c_{2}\) for every \(w\), so the effective step is sandwiched: \[
c_{1}\alpha_{k}\leq\bar{\alpha}_{k}\leq c_{2}\alpha_{k}.
\] Hypothesis 2 gives \(\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}=\infty\) and \(\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}^{2}<\infty\); the sandwich transfers both to \(\bar{\alpha}_{k}\), since \(\sum\bar{\alpha}_{k}\geq c_{1}\sum\alpha_{k}=\infty\) and \(\sum\bar{\alpha}_{k}^{2}\leq c_{2}^{2}\sum\alpha_{k}^{2}<\infty\). And \(\sum_{k}\beta_{k}^{2}=\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}^{2}<\infty\).
Condition 2. Hypothesis 3 gives \(\E[\eta_{k}\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]=0\) and the uniform bound \(\E[\eta_{k}^{2}\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]\leq C\), which is what Theorem 2.2 asks for; pointwise finiteness at each \(k\) would not be enough, since the constant must not drift with \(k\). Negating \(\eta_{k}\) changes neither.
Both conditions hold, so Theorem 2.2 gives \(\Delta_{k}\to0\) almost surely, that is \(w_{k}\to w^{*}\). \(\square\)









Note



The effective step \(\bar{\alpha}_{k}\) depends on \(w_{k}'\), so the proof requires the history-dependent steps allowed by Theorem 2.2.




Mean estimation is Robbins-Monro
The claim that Equation 2.9 converges now follows from Theorem 2.1 in three steps.

Write mean estimation as root-finding. Define \[
g(w)=w-\E[X],
\] whose root is \(w^{*}=\E[X]\). Its value is unknown because it contains the mean being estimated.
Identify the noisy observation. With a sample \(x\) in hand we can evaluate \[
\tilde{g}(w,x)=w-x,
\] which is exactly \(g\) plus zero-mean noise: \[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{g}(w,x)&=w-x\\
&=w-x+\E[X]-\E[X]\\
&=\underbrace{\big(w-\E[X]\big)}_{g(w)}+\underbrace{\big(\E[X]-x\big)}_{\eta}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Apply RM. Substituting into Equation 2.10, \[
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}\,\tilde{g}(w_{k},x_{k})=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}(w_{k}-x_{k}),
\] which is precisely Equation 2.9. Its convergence follows from Theorem 2.1.







Note



Check the hypotheses hold here: \(\nabla_{w}g(w)=1\), so condition 1 is satisfied with \(c_{1}=c_{2}=1\); and \(\eta=\E[X]-x\) has mean zero by construction, so condition 3 holds whenever \(X\) has finite variance. Condition 2 constrains the chosen step sizes.




One sample stream, three step-size rules, run through @eq-mean-general
fig, ax = new_ax(6.6, 4.4)
mu, sigma, n = 1.0, 1.0, 400
x = RNG.normal(mu, sigma, n)  # one shared sample stream
k = np.arange(1, n + 1)

ax.axhline(mu, color=GREY, lw=0.9, ls="--", zorder=2)

for alpha, colour in ((0.30, COL["orange"]), (0.10, COL["sky"])):
    w = mean_estimation_path(x, alpha, w0=5.0)
    ax.plot(np.arange(n + 1), w, color=colour, lw=1.0, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
    # stationary std of the constant-step recursion: sigma * sqrt(a/(2-a))
    band = sigma * np.sqrt(alpha / (2 - alpha))
    ax.fill_between([0, n], mu - band, mu + band, color=colour, alpha=0.10, zorder=1)

w = mean_estimation_path(x, 1.0 / k, w0=5.0)
ax.plot(np.arange(n + 1), w, color=COL["vermilion"], lw=2.2, zorder=5)

ax.set_xlim(0, n * 1.13)  # headroom on the right for the E[X] tag
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 5.3)
ax.set_xlabel(r"iteration $k$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$w_k$")
# Direct labels live in the empty upper-right quadrant, clear of the paths.
label_at(ax, n * 1.015, mu + 0.28, r"$\mathbb{E}[X]$", color=INK, fontsize=9.5)
label_at(ax, n * 0.50, 4.75, r"constant $\alpha=0.3$", color=COL["orange"], fontsize=9.5)
label_at(ax, n * 0.50, 4.25, r"constant $\alpha=0.1$", color=COL["sky"], fontsize=9.5)
label_at(ax, n * 0.50, 3.75, r"$\alpha_k=1/k$", color=COL["vermilion"], fontsize=9.5)
label_at(
    ax,
    n * 0.50,
    3.20,
    "shaded: stationary band\n" r"$\sigma\sqrt{\alpha/(2-\alpha)}$",
    color=GREY,
    fontsize=8.5,
    va="top",
)
ax.set_title(r"Why $\sum_k \alpha_k^2 < \infty$ is the condition that makes it settle")
plt.show()








Figure 2.2: The recursion Equation 2.9 uses one stream of draws \(x_k\sim N(1,1)\) and starts at \(w_1=5\). With \(\alpha_k=1/k\) (thick), the estimate converges to \(\E[X]\). Constant steps retain fluctuations under this sampling noise. Shading marks one stationary standard deviation, \(\sigma\sqrt{\alpha/(2-\alpha)}\), on either side of the mean; larger steps give wider bands.







Stochastic gradient descent
Applying the same argument to a gradient gives stochastic gradient descent. Suppose we want to minimize
\[
J(w)=\E\big[f(w,X)\big]
\tag{2.12}\]
over \(w\), where the expectation is over a random variable \(X\) we can sample but whose distribution we do not know. There are three ways to descend.



Table 2.3: Gradient estimates for Equation 2.12.











Update
Needs




Gradient descent
\(w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}\,\E[\nabla_{w}f(w_{k},X)]\)
the distribution of \(X\), to take the expectation


Batch gradient descent
\(w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\nabla_{w}f(w_{k},x_{i})\)
\(n\) samples per step


Stochastic gradient descent
\(w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}\,\nabla_{w}f(w_{k},x_{k})\)
one sample per step






The last row is stochastic gradient descent (SGD):
\[
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}\,\nabla_{w}f(w_{k},x_{k}).
\tag{2.13}\]
It replaces the true gradient with a noisy single-sample estimate. Its convergence follows from Theorem 2.1 under that theorem’s assumptions.






NoteDerivation: SGD is Robbins-Monro on the first-order condition





Minimizing Equation 2.12 means solving its first-order condition, which is a root-finding problem in the sense of the previous section: \[
g(w)\defeq\nabla_{w}J(w)=\E\big[\nabla_{w}f(w,X)\big]=0 ,
\] where the interchange of \(\nabla_{w}\) and \(\E\) assumes \(f(\cdot,x)\) is differentiable and that \(\|\nabla_{w}f(w,X)\|\) is dominated near \(w\) by an integrable envelope, so dominated convergence applies to the difference quotients. We cannot evaluate \(g\), since it is an expectation over an unknown distribution. But with a sample \(x\) in hand we can evaluate \(\nabla_{w}f(w,x)\), and it is \(g\) plus zero-mean noise: \[
\tilde{g}(w,x)=\nabla_{w}f(w,x)
=\underbrace{\E\big[\nabla_{w}f(w,X)\big]}_{g(w)}
+\underbrace{\Big(\nabla_{w}f(w,x)-\E\big[\nabla_{w}f(w,X)\big]\Big)}_{\eta} .
\] Substituting into the RM algorithm Equation 2.10 gives exactly Equation 2.13. SGD is RM applied to a gradient, with the three convergence conditions of Theorem 2.1 imposed on \(g=\nabla_{w}J\).




Example 2.1 (Mean estimation is SGD) Take \(f(w,x)=\tfrac{1}{2}|w-x|^{2}\), so that \(J(w)=\tfrac{1}{2}\E|w-X|^{2}\) is minimized at \(w^{*}=\E[X]\). Then \(\nabla_{w}f(w,x)=w-x\), and Equation 2.13 reads \[
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\alpha_{k}(w_{k}-x_{k}),
\] which is Equation 2.9 once more. Mean estimation is a special case of SGD, which is a special case of Robbins-Monro.

title: 3  Temporal Difference Learning, Sarsa, and Q-learning
text:
3.1 Incremental versus episodic learning
Chapter 2’s policy evaluation step was Equation 2.7, the average return over \(N\) episodes. Written as a running average in the manner of Equation 2.8, the \(j\)-th update is
\[
q_{\pi_{k}}^{j+1}(s,a)=q_{\pi_{k}}^{j}(s,a)+\frac{1}{j}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t}^{j},a_{t}^{j})-q_{\pi_{k}}^{j}(s,a)\right].
\tag{3.1}\]
The return is available after \(T\). Incremental updates have the form
\[
q_{t+1}(s_{t},a_{t})=q_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})+\alpha_{t}\times(\text{something available at time } t),
\tag{3.2}\]
where \(q_{t}\) is the time-\(t\) estimate of \(q_{\pi_{k}}\).

title: 3  Temporal Difference Learning, Sarsa, and Q-learning
text:
Definition 3.1 (Incremental and episodic learning) An algorithm is incremental if it updates in real time, at every transition, as in Equation 3.2. It is episodic (or non-incremental) if it must wait for an episode to finish, as in Equation 3.1.







WarningA terminology trap



Sutton and Barto call this same distinction online versus offline. Here we use incremental and episodic because “offline RL” has since come to mean something else entirely: learning from a fixed, previously collected dataset with no further interaction.

title: 3  Temporal Difference Learning, Sarsa, and Q-learning
text:
3.2 TD learning of state values
Estimate \(v_{\pi}\) for a fixed policy \(\pi\), with no improvement step. Write \(v_{t}(s)\) for the time-\(t\) estimate of \(v_{\pi}(s)\).
Let \(\mathcal H_t\) contain the history through \(s_t\), before drawing the current action under \(\pi\) and the next transition. Use \(\mathcal H_t\)-measurable effective step sizes: \(\alpha_t(s)=0\) for \(s\ne s_t\) and \(0<\alpha_t(s_t)\le1\). All step-size sums below use this convention.






NoteAlgorithm: TD learning of state values



Given experience \(\{(s_{t},r_{t+1},s_{t+1})\}_{t}\) generated by following \(\pi\), at each \(t=0,1,2,\dots\)
\[
v_{t+1}(s_{t})=v_{t}(s_{t})+\alpha_{t}(s_{t})\big[\,r_{t+1}+\gamma v_{t}(s_{t+1})-v_{t}(s_{t})\,\big],
\tag{3.3}\]
\[
v_{t+1}(s)=v_{t}(s)\qquad\text{for all } s\neq s_{t}.
\tag{3.4}\]


Annotating Equation 3.3 names its parts:
\[
\underbrace{v_{t+1}(s_{t})}_{\text{new estimate}}
=\underbrace{v_{t}(s_{t})}_{\text{current estimate}}
+\alpha_{t}(s_{t})\Big[\underbrace{\overbrace{r_{t+1}+\gamma v_{t}(s_{t+1})}^{\text{TD target }\bar{v}_{t}}-v_{t}(s_{t})}_{\text{TD error }\delta_{t}}\Big].
\tag{3.5}\]

Definition 3.2 (TD target and TD error) \[
\bar{v}_{t}\defeq r_{t+1}+\gamma v_{t}(s_{t+1}),
\qquad
\delta_{t}\defeq \bar{v}_{t}-v_{t}(s_{t}).
\]

This extends Equation 1.3 to state-dependent step sizes.

Why \(\bar{v}_{t}\) deserves the name “target”






NoteDerivation: the update contracts the gap to the target





Rewrite Equation 3.3 in terms of \(\bar{v}_{t}\) and subtract \(\bar{v}_{t}\) from both sides: \[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t+1}(s_{t})&=v_{t}(s_{t})+\alpha_{t}(s_{t})\big[\bar{v}_{t}-v_{t}(s_{t})\big]\\
\implies\quad v_{t+1}(s_{t})-\bar{v}_{t}&=v_{t}(s_{t})-\bar{v}_{t}+\alpha_{t}(s_{t})\big[\bar{v}_{t}-v_{t}(s_{t})\big]\\
\implies\quad v_{t+1}(s_{t})-\bar{v}_{t}&=\big[1-\alpha_{t}(s_{t})\big]\big[v_{t}(s_{t})-\bar{v}_{t}\big]\\
\implies\quad \big|v_{t+1}(s_{t})-\bar{v}_{t}\big|&=\big|1-\alpha_{t}(s_{t})\big|\,\big|v_{t}(s_{t})-\bar{v}_{t}\big| .
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(0<\alpha_t(s_t)\le1\), we have \(0\le1-\alpha_t(s_t)<1\), and therefore \[
\big|v_{t+1}(s_{t})-\bar{v}_{t}\big|\leq\big|v_{t}(s_{t})-\bar{v}_{t}\big| .
\]



Each update strictly shrinks the distance to \(\bar v_t\) when the distance is nonzero. At \(\alpha_t>2\), the factor \(|1-\alpha_t|\) exceeds one and the distance grows. The target itself changes with \(v_t\).


Convergence

Theorem 3.1 (Convergence of TD learning) Assume \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), finite \(\mathcal{S}\), bounded rewards, a fixed policy \(\pi\), and the effective step sizes defined above. Then under Equation 3.3, \(v_t(s)\to v_\pi(s)\) almost surely for every \(s\), provided the following conditions hold almost surely: \[
\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}(s)=\infty
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}^{2}(s)<\infty
\qquad\text{for all } s\in\mathcal{S}.
\]

These are the Robbins-Monro conditions of Theorem 2.1, imposed separately at each state.
The proof uses a multi-variable variant of Theorem 2.2, with one variable per state. It allows noise bias bounded by the current error and adds the requirement \(\E[\beta_{k}]\leq\E[\alpha_{k}]\), which the Chapter 2 form does not impose. Neither theorem contains the other; the Robbins-Monro corollary uses the Chapter 2 form.

Theorem 3.2 (Dvoretzky, multi-variable form) Let \(\mathcal S\) be a finite index set and \(\{\mathcal H_k\}\) a filtration. Assume \(\Delta_k\), \(\alpha_k\), and \(\beta_k\) are \(\mathcal H_k\)-measurable, with \(0\le\alpha_k(s)\le1\) and \(\beta_k(s)\ge0\). For the stochastic process \[
\Delta_{k+1}(s)=\big(1-\alpha_{k}(s)\big)\Delta_{k}(s)+\beta_{k}(s)\eta_{k}(s),
\tag{3.6}\] \(\Delta_{k}(s)\) converges to zero almost surely for every \(s\in\mathcal{S}\) provided that, for every \(s\in\mathcal{S}\),

\(\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}(s)=\infty\), \(\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}^{2}(s)<\infty\), \(\sum_{k}\beta_{k}^{2}(s)<\infty\), and \(\E[\beta_{k}(s)\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]\leq\E[\alpha_{k}(s)\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]\), uniformly almost surely;
\(\big\|\E[\eta_{k}(s)\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]\big\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|\Delta_{k}\|_{\infty}\) for some \(\gamma\in(0,1)\);
\(\operatorname{var}[\eta_{k}(s)\given\mathcal{H}_{k}]\leq C\big(1+\|\Delta_{k}\|_{\infty}\big)^{2}\) for a constant \(C\),

where \(\|x(s)\|_{\infty}\defeq\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}|x(s)|\) is the maximum over the index set.







Tip



Condition 2 allows conditional bias bounded by \(\gamma<1\) times the current error. For TD, \(\gamma\) is the discount factor.








NoteProof of the convergence of TD learning





Fix an arbitrary state \(s\in\mathcal{S}\) and define the estimation error \[
\Delta_{t}(s)\defeq v_{t}(s)-v_{\pi}(s).
\]
Step 1: put the algorithm in the form Equation 3.6. When \(s=s_{t}\), subtract \(v_{\pi}(s)\) from both sides of Equation 3.3: \[
\Delta_{t+1}(s)=\big(1-\alpha_{t}(s)\big)\Delta_{t}(s)+\alpha_{t}(s)\underbrace{\big[r_{t+1}+\gamma v_{t}(s_{t+1})-v_{\pi}(s)\big]}_{\eta_{t}(s)} .
\] When \(s\neq s_{t}\), Equation 3.4 gives \(\Delta_{t+1}(s)=\Delta_{t}(s)\), which is the same expression with \(\alpha_{t}(s)=0\) and \(\eta_{t}(s)=0\). So regardless of which state was visited, \[
\Delta_{t+1}(s)=\big(1-\alpha_{t}(s)\big)\Delta_{t}(s)+\alpha_{t}(s)\eta_{t}(s),
\] which is Equation 3.6 with \(\beta_{t}(s)=\alpha_{t}(s)\), so the requirement \(\E[\beta_{t}]\leq\E[\alpha_{t}]\) holds with equality.
Step 2: condition 1. This is precisely the hypothesis of Theorem 3.1.
Step 3: condition 2, the contraction. Conditioning on \(\mathcal{H}_{t}\) fixes \(v_{t}\) and \(s_{t}\). The remaining randomness is \((r_{t+1},s_{t+1})\), whose law under the fixed policy depends on \(s_{t}\). For \(s\neq s_{t}\), \(\eta_{t}(s)=0\) and the bound is trivial. For \(s=s_{t}\), \[
\E[\eta_{t}(s)\given\mathcal{H}_{t}]=\E\big[r_{t+1}+\gamma v_{t}(s_{t+1})\given\mathcal{H}_{t}\big]-v_{\pi}(s_{t}).
\] Now use the Bellman equation for \(v_{\pi}\), which says \(v_{\pi}(s_{t})=\E[r_{t+1}+\gamma v_{\pi}(s_{t+1})\given s_{t}]\). Subtracting, the reward terms cancel exactly and only the value gap survives: \[
\E[\eta_{t}(s)\given\mathcal{H}_{t}]=\gamma\,\E\big[v_{t}(s_{t+1})-v_{\pi}(s_{t+1})\given\mathcal{H}_{t}\big]
=\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p(s'\given s_{t})\big[v_{t}(s')-v_{\pi}(s')\big],
\] where \(v_{t}\) passes outside the expectation because \(\mathcal{H}_{t}\) determines it. Bound the sum by its largest term, using that \(p(\cdot\given s_{t})\) is a probability distribution and therefore sums to one: \[
\big|\E[\eta_{t}(s)\given\mathcal{H}_{t}]\big|
\leq\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\given s_{t})\max_{s'}\big|v_{t}(s')-v_{\pi}(s')\big|
=\gamma\max_{s'}\big|v_{t}(s')-v_{\pi}(s')\big|
=\gamma\|\Delta_{t}\|_{\infty}.
\] This holds whether or not \(s=s_{t}\), so \(\|\E[\eta_{t}(s)\given\mathcal{H}_{t}]\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|\Delta_{t}\|_{\infty}\), with \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) the discount factor. Note both sides are \(\mathcal{H}_{t}\)-measurable random variables, which is exactly the form condition 2 of Theorem 3.2 asks for.
Step 4: condition 3. For \(s\ne s_t\), \(\operatorname{var}[\eta_t(s)\given\mathcal H_t]=0\). For \(s=s_t\), subtracting \(v_\pi(s_t)\) leaves \(\operatorname{var}[r_{t+1}+\gamma v_t(s_{t+1})\given\mathcal H_t]\). This is bounded by a constant multiple of \((1+\|\Delta_t\|_\infty)^2\): rewards and \(v_\pi\) are bounded, and \(\|v_t\|_\infty\le\|v_\pi\|_\infty+\|\Delta_t\|_\infty\).
All three conditions hold, so Theorem 3.2 gives \(\Delta_{t}(s)\to0\) almost surely for every \(s\). \(\square\)









Important



At \(\gamma=1\), the strict contraction argument in Step 3 is unavailable.








TipWhat the two conditions demand here



Recall from Equation 3.4 that \(\alpha_{t}(s)>0\) only when \(s_{t}=s\), and \(\alpha_{t}(s)=0\) otherwise. So:

\(\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}(s)=\infty\) for every \(s\) can only hold if every state is visited infinitely often. Thus the step-size condition also imposes an exploration requirement, which is why \(\eps\)-greedy policies from Definition 2.2 reappear the moment we start improving the policy.
\(\sum_t\alpha_t^2(s)<\infty\) requires the steps on visits to \(s\) to vanish. With a small constant step and persistent sampling noise, a stable recursion generally keeps fluctuating, as in Figure 2.2. A constant-step deterministic contraction can still converge; the theorem supplies sufficient conditions for the noisy case.





TD against Monte Carlo



Table 3.1: Timing and data requirements of TD and Monte Carlo; see Table 1.1 for bias and variance.











TD / Sarsa
Monte Carlo




Timing
incremental: updates immediately after each reward
episodic: waits until an episode is complete


Task type
handles episodic and continuing tasks
complete returns for terminating tasks; finite rollouts of continuing tasks need tail control


Bootstrapping
yes: the update uses the previous estimate of the same value, so it needs an initial guess
no: estimates values directly from returns, no initial guess needed


Sampling noise

3.3 Sarsa: TD learning of action values
For model-free policy search, apply TD to action values.






NoteAlgorithm: Sarsa



Given experience \(\{(s_{t},a_{t},r_{t+1},s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\}_{t}\) generated by following \(\pi\),
\[
q_{t+1}(s_{t},a_{t})=q_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})+\alpha_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})\big[\,r_{t+1}+\gamma q_{t}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})-q_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})\,\big],
\tag{3.7}\]
with \(q_{t+1}(s,a)=q_{t}(s,a)\) for all \((s,a)\neq(s_{t},a_{t})\).


The name comes from the update’s quintuple \((s_{t},a_{t},r_{t+1},s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\): state, action, reward, state, action.
Equation 3.7 is a stochastic approximation algorithm, in the sense of Theorem 2.1, for the equation
\[
q_{\pi}(s,a)=\E\big[R+\gamma q_{\pi}(S',A')\ \given\ s,a\big],
\qquad\text{for all } s,a,
\tag{3.8}\]
which is the action-value form of the policy-evaluation Bellman equation for the fixed policy \(\pi\): Equation 2.2 with the maximization over \(\pi\) removed.






NoteProof that the Sarsa fixed point is the Bellman equation





Write \(p(r\given s,a)\) for the distribution of the immediate reward and \(p(s'\given s,a)\) for the transition, both conditional on the pair \((s,a)\). Expanding the right-hand side of Equation 3.8 by the definition of expectation,
\[
\E\big[R+\gamma q_{\pi}(S',A')\given s,a\big]
=\sum_{r}r\,p(r\given s,a)
+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{a'\in\mathcal{A}}q_{\pi}(s',a')\,p(s',a'\given s,a).
\]
Linearity separates the expectations over \(R\) and \(S'\) using their marginal distributions, without an independence assumption. The first term is the expected immediate reward, which collapses to \(r(s,a)\) whenever the reward is a deterministic function of the pair, as it was in Chapters 1 and 2. The second term needs the joint law of the next state and the next action.
Factor the joint. By the chain rule: \[
p(s',a'\given s,a)=p(s'\given s,a)\,p(a'\given s',s,a).
\] The second factor is where the policy enters. The agent produces \(a'\) by drawing from \(\pi(\cdot\given s')\), using a stationary Markov policy \(\pi\) that depends only on the current state. So conditionally on \(s'\), the next action is independent of \((s,a)\), and \[
p(a'\given s',s,a)=p(a'\given s')=\pi(a'\given s').
\] For a history-dependent policy, this factorization need not hold; \(q\) would generally require history as an additional argument beyond \((s,a)\).
Substitute and collect. Putting the factorization back and summing over \(a'\) first, \[
q_{\pi}(s,a)=\underbrace{\sum_{r}r\,p(r\given s,a)}_{\E[R\given s,a]}
+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p(s'\given s,a)\underbrace{\sum_{a'\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a'\given s')\,q_{\pi}(s',a')}_{v_{\pi}(s')},
\] because the action value averaged against the policy at \(s'\) is by definition the state value there. Hence \[
q_{\pi}(s,a)=\E[R\given s,a]+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p(s'\given s,a)\,v_{\pi}(s'),
\] which is Equation 2.5, the model-based form of the action value.
And back to state values. Average that last display against \(\pi(a\given s)\) and use Definition 2.1: \[
v_{\pi}(s)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\given s)\,q_{\pi}(s,a)
=r_{\pi}(s)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p_{\pi}(s'\given s)\,v_{\pi}(s'),
\] which is Equation 1.6, the policy-evaluation equation, written one state at a time. \(\square\)



Sarsa samples \((r_{t+1},s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\) in Equation 3.8 and substitutes \(q_{t}\) for the unknown \(q_{\pi}\) in the target.

Theorem 3.3 (Convergence of Sarsa) For a fixed policy \(\pi\), assume \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), finite \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal A\), and bounded rewards. Here \(\mathcal H_t\) includes the current \((s_t,a_t)\) but precedes the next reward, state, and action. Use \(\mathcal H_t\)-measurable step sizes, with \(\alpha_t(s,a)=0\) for unvisited pairs and \(0<\alpha_t(s_t,a_t)\le1\). Then Equation 3.7 gives \(q_t(s,a)\to q_\pi(s,a)\) almost surely for every pair if \(\sum_t\alpha_t(s,a)=\infty\) and \(\sum_t\alpha_t^2(s,a)<\infty\) almost surely for every \((s,a)\).







NoteProof of the convergence of Sarsa





The proof of Theorem 3.1 carries over from states to state-action pairs with the following substitutions.
The index set. Replace \(\mathcal{S}\) by \(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\) everywhere. It is still finite, which is all Theorem 3.2 ever asked of it, and the norm becomes \(\|x\|_{\infty}=\max_{(s,a)}|x(s,a)|\), a maximum over pairs.
Step 1, the error process. In place of \(\Delta_{t}(s)\defeq v_{t}(s)-v_{\pi}(s)\), define \(\Delta_{t}(s,a)\defeq q_{t}(s,a)-q_{\pi}(s,a)\). Subtracting \(q_{\pi}(s,a)\) from Equation 3.7 when \((s,a)=(s_{t},a_{t})\) gives \[
\Delta_{t+1}(s,a)=\big(1-\alpha_{t}(s,a)\big)\Delta_{t}(s,a)+\alpha_{t}(s,a)\underbrace{\big[r_{t+1}+\gamma q_{t}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})-q_{\pi}(s,a)\big]}_{\eta_{t}(s,a)},
\] and every other pair is left untouched, which is the same line with \(\alpha_{t}(s,a)=0\) and \(\eta_{t}(s,a)=0\). That is Equation 3.6 on the new index set, again with \(\beta_{t}=\alpha_{t}\).
Step 2, condition 1. The hypothesis of the theorem, now imposed on pairs.
Step 3, the contraction. Conditioning on \(\mathcal H_t\) fixes \(q_t\) and \((s_t,a_t)\). The remaining randomness is the next reward, state, and action under the fixed policy \(\pi\). The bound is trivial for unvisited pairs. For \((s,a)=(s_t,a_t)\), \[
\E[\eta_t(s,a)\given\mathcal H_t]
=\E\big[r_{t+1}+\gamma q_t(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\given\mathcal H_t\big]-q_\pi(s_t,a_t).
\] Subtracting Equation 3.8 cancels the reward terms, as in the proof for \(v_{\pi}\), and leaves the error at the next pair: \[
\E[\eta_t(s,a)\given\mathcal H_t]
=\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal S}\sum_{a'\in\mathcal A}
p(s'\given s_t,a_t)\,\pi(a'\given s')\big[q_t(s',a')-q_\pi(s',a')\big].
\] The joint probabilities \(p(s',a'\given s_{t},a_{t})\) are nonnegative and sum to one, so \[
\big|\E[\eta_t(s,a)\given\mathcal H_t]\big|
\le\gamma\max_{(s',a')}\big|q_t(s',a')-q_\pi(s',a')\big|
=\gamma\|\Delta_t\|_\infty,
\] where \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) is the discount factor.
Step 4, the variance. The constant \(q_{\pi}(s,a)\) drops out of the variance, \(r_{t+1}\) is bounded, and \(q_{t}\) differs from the fixed \(q_{\pi}\) by at most \(\|\Delta_{t}\|_{\infty}\), so condition 3 holds.
All three conditions of Theorem 3.2 hold on the index set \(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\), so \(\Delta_{t}(s,a)\to0\) almost surely for every pair. \(\square\)









WarningExploration over state-action pairs



Since \(\alpha_{t}(s,a)>0\) only when \((s_{t},a_{t})=(s,a)\), the condition \(\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}(s,a)=\infty\) for every pair requires infinitely many visits to each pair. A fixed deterministic policy can visit every state in \(\mathcal{S}\) infinitely often while sampling one action per state, leaving \(|\mathcal{S}|(|\mathcal{A}|-1)\) entries with \(\alpha_{t}=0\) at every \(t\). These entries retain their initial values. With \(|\mathcal A|>1\), the policy cannot meet the pairwise visitation condition.


The theorem evaluates \(q_{\pi}\) for a fixed policy \(\pi\). Policy search also requires an improvement step.

Policy searching by Sarsa
The evaluation and improvement steps of Equation 2.3 are interleaved: take one TD step, improve the policy, and generate the next transition.






NoteAlgorithm: policy searching by Sarsa



For each episode: generate \(a_{0}\) at \(s_{0}\) following \(\pi_{0}(s_{0})\). Then for each \(t=0,1,2,\dots\) while \(s_{t}\) is not the target state:

Interact. Take \(a_{t}\), observe \(r_{t+1}\) and \(s_{t+1}\), and generate \(a_{t+1}\) following \(\pi_{t}(s_{t+1})\).
Update the \(q\)-value of \((s_{t},a_{t})\) by Equation 3.7.
Update the policy at \(s_{t}\) to be \(\eps\)-greedy with respect to the new \(q_{t+1}\), in the sense of Definition 2.2.
Set \(s_{t}\leftarrow s_{t+1}\), \(a_{t}\leftarrow a_{t+1}\).









NoteImplementation: eps-greedy action selection





For the two-action chain in Figure 3.1, \(|\mathcal{A}|=2\), so Definition 2.2 assigns \(1-\eps/2\) to the greedy action and \(\eps/2\) to the other. Here q is the table, g selects its larger entry at s, and \(\eps=0.2\).

def eps_greedy(q, s):
    """The eps-greedy policy of @def-eps-greedy at s, for the two actions here."""
    g = int(q[s, 1] > q[s, 0])
    return 1 - g if RNG.random() < EPS / 2 else g

3.4 Q-learning: TD learning of optimal action values
Sarsa estimates \(q_{\pi}\) for the policy currently being followed, and therefore must be combined with an improvement step. Q-learning skips the intermediary and estimates \(q^{*}\) directly.






NoteAlgorithm: Q-learning



\[
q_{t+1}(s_{t},a_{t})=q_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})+\alpha_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})\Big[\,r_{t+1}+\gamma\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q_{t}(s_{t+1},a)-q_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})\,\Big],
\tag{3.9}\]
with \(q_{t+1}(s,a)=q_{t}(s,a)\) for all \((s,a)\neq(s_{t},a_{t})\).








NoteImplementation: Sarsa and Q-learning, one loop





The loop for Figure 3.1 uses step(s, a) to return the next state, reward, and termination flag. There are N_DEC = 4 decision states and \(\gamma=0.9\). use_max selects the \(\max\) target of Equation 3.9 or the next action drawn by eps_greedy for Equation 3.7; Sarsa then takes that same action. Both use \(\alpha_{t}=1/n(s,a)\) and uniform starting states. qs, vals, and checks record the plotted outcomes.

def run(use_max, n_ep, checks):
    """One learning run; `use_max` selects the TD target of @tbl-sarsa-q.

    use_max=True is Q-learning @eq-qlearning, whose target maxes over the table.
    use_max=False is Sarsa @eq-sarsa, whose target uses the action a_{t+1} that the
    eps-greedy behavior policy actually draws. Everything else is shared.

    Both algorithms use uniform starting states and steps 1/n(s, a).
    Separate runs consume different random draws and generate different trajectories;
    the start distribution is shared, not the realized state-action visits.
    """
    q = RNG.normal(0.0, 1e-3, (N_DEC, 2))  # jitter only breaks the initial ties
    n = np.zeros((N_DEC, 2))               # visit counts, so alpha = 1 / n(s, a)
    wanted = set(checks.tolist())
    qs, vals = [], []
    for ep in range(1, n_ep + 1):
        s = int(RNG.integers(N_DEC))       # uniform state starts, not exploring starts:
        #                                   the first action is still drawn eps-greedily
        a = eps_greedy(q, s)
        while True:
            s2, r, done = step(s, a)
            if done:
                target = r
            elif use_max:
                target = r + GAMMA * q[s2].max()   # Q-learning: max over the table
            else:
                a2 = eps_greedy(q, s2)             # Sarsa: the action drawn next,
                target = r + GAMMA * q[s2, a2]     # read before the update
            n[s, a] += 1
            q[s, a] += (target - q[s, a]) / n[s, a]
            if done:
                break
            s, a = s2, (eps_greedy(q, s2) if use_max else a2)
        if ep in wanted:
            qs.append(q.copy())
            vals.append(policy_value(q[:, 1] > q[:, 0]))
    return np.array(qs), np.array(vals)







Table 3.2: Sarsa and Q-learning use different TD targets.










TD target




Sarsa
\(r_{t+1}+\gamma\,q_{t}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\)


Q-learning
\(r_{t+1}+\gamma\,\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q_{t}(s_{t+1},a)\)






That single substitution changes what equation the algorithm solves. Sarsa is stochastic approximation on the Bellman equation Equation 3.8; Q-learning is stochastic approximation on the Bellman optimality equation,
\[
q(s,a)=\E\Big[R+\gamma\max_{a'\in\mathcal{A}}q(S',a')\ \given\ s,a\Big],
\qquad\text{for all } s,a,
\tag{3.10}\]
whose solution is \(q^{*}\).






NoteProof that the Q-learning fixed point is the Bellman optimality equation





Step 1: expand the expectation. Exactly as for Sarsa, write the right-hand side as sums against the conditional distributions of the reward and of the next state. What differs is that the next action is not random: the \(\max\) has already chosen it, so only \(r\) and \(s'\) are integrated out and no policy is needed to average over \(a'\), \[
q(s,a)=\sum_{r}r\,p(r\given s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p(s'\given s,a)\max_{a'\in\mathcal{A}}q(s',a').
\] Step 2: maximize both sides over the first action. Both sides are functions of \(a\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) is finite, so the maximum exists and \[
\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q(s,a)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Big\{\sum_{r}r\,p(r\given s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p(s'\given s,a)\max_{a'\in\mathcal{A}}q(s',a')\Big\}.
\]
Step 3: name the maximized value. Define \[
v(s)\defeq\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q(s,a).
\] The inner maximum on the right is that same definition evaluated at \(s'\), so it is \(v(s')\), and the left-hand side is \(v(s)\): \[
v(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Big\{\sum_{r}r\,p(r\given s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p(s'\given s,a)\,v(s')\Big\},
\] which is Equation 1.4, using \(\gamma\) and the expected reward.
Step 4: maximizing over actions is maximizing over policies. Chapter 2 wrote the optimality equation with the maximum taken over stochastic policies, Equation 2.1, so the two forms still have to be reconciled. Abbreviate the bracket in Step 3 as \[
f(a)\defeq\sum_{r}r\,p(r\given s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}p(s'\given s,a)\,v(s').
\] For any distribution \(\pi(\cdot\given s)\) on the finite set \(\mathcal{A}\), \[
\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\given s)f(a)\leq\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\given s)\max_{b\in\mathcal{A}}f(b)=\max_{b\in\mathcal{A}}f(b),
\] since a weighted average of finitely many numbers cannot exceed the largest of them, the weights summing to one. The bound is attained: finiteness of \(\mathcal{A}\) makes \(\argmax_{a}f(a)\) nonempty, and putting all the mass on one of its elements turns the average into the maximum. Hence \[
\max_{\pi}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\given s)f(a)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}f(a),
\] the maximum over the simplex of distributions being attained at a vertex, that is, at a point mass. Step 3 is therefore Equation 2.1, and Equation 3.10 is the Bellman optimality equation written one state-action pair at a time. \(\square\)



An optimal policy is \(\pi(s)=\argmax_{a}q^{*}(s,a)\); the \(\eps\)-greedy behavior policy supplies exploration. Conversely, define \(q\) from a solution \(v\) of Equation 1.4 by Step 1’s one-step formula. Then \(\max_{a}q(s,a)=v(s)\), and substitution gives Equation 3.10. Thus the fixed points determine each other, with \(v^{*}(s)=\max_{a}q^{*}(s,a)\).

Why Q-learning is off-policy
The updates require different data. Sarsa Equation 3.7 needs \(a_{t+1}\), the action the current policy will actually take next. Q-learning Equation 3.9 does not: the \(\max\) is taken over the table, not over what happens. Its update needs only \((s_{t},a_{t},r_{t+1},s_{t+1})\).

Definition 3.3 (On-policy and off-policy) An algorithm is on-policy if the data must be generated by the policy being learned. It is off-policy if the data may come from any behavior policy, while the target policy being learned is a different one.

Sarsa is on-policy: \(a_{t+1}\) ties the update to the policy in force. Q-learning is off-policy: its convergence theorem permits an exploratory behavior policy, with every state-action pair sampled infinitely often and the required step sizes. Stored transitions can also be used for updates; their coverage limits what can be learned.






NoteAlgorithm: policy searching by Q-learning



For each episode, for each \(t=0,1,2,\dots\) while \(s_{t}\) is not the target state:

Interact. Generate \(a_{t}\) following \(\pi_{t}(s_{t})\); observe \(r_{t+1}\) and \(s_{t+1}\).
Update the \(q\)-value of \((s_{t},a_{t})\) by Equation 3.9.
Update the policy at \(s_{t}\) to be \(\eps\)-greedy with respect to \(q_{t+1}\).









Tip



The behavior policy here changes with the \(q\) table. The target remains \(\max_a q(s_{t+1},a)\), so this implementation is off-policy too. A fixed exploratory behavior policy is another way to collect the required transitions.
