title: 5  State Abstraction
text:
5.1 Q-learning on abstract states
In Chapter 3’s Q-learning update, a transition \((s_t,a_t,r_{t+1},s_{t+1})\) revises the estimate \(q_t(s_t,a_t)\). The row that changes is the one for \(s_t\). Giving several states one row reduces the number of entries to estimate and lets visits to any of those states update that row. We want to know when these shared estimates can recover the optimal action values and when they suffice to choose an optimal action.
We use the finite discounted MDP of Chapters 1–3, with state space \(\mathcal S\), the same finite action set \(\mathcal A\) at every state, bounded rewards, and \(0<\gamma<1\). Call a state \(s\) of this MDP a full state.
Like the feature map in Chapter 3, \(\phi\) represents a state in a form that the learner uses to estimate values. Here the label selects one row, giving a table with \(|\overline{\mathcal S}|\,|\mathcal A|\) entries. The definition follows Li, Walsh, and Littman (2006), §3.1.
Write \(x_t=\phi(s_t)\) and let \(\bar q_t(x,a)\) be the table indexed by abstract state and action. In Equation 3.9, replace the two state arguments with \(x_t\) and \(x_{t+1}\). Let \(\alpha_t(x,a)\) be the step size for entry \((x,a)\). The TD error \(\delta_t\) and the update are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_t
  &=r_{t+1}+\gamma\max_{b\in\mathcal A}\bar q_t(x_{t+1},b)-\bar q_t(x_t,a_t),\\
\bar q_{t+1}(x_t,a_t)
  &=\bar q_t(x_t,a_t)+\alpha_t(x_t,a_t)\delta_t .
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.1}\]
Two full states with the same label now update the same entry for a given action. To see when those updates agree in expectation, first compute the probability of the next label \(y\). It is the sum of the transition probabilities to the full states in its group,
\[
p_\phi(y\given s,a)
=\sum_{s'\in\mathcal S_y}p(s'\given s,a).
\tag{5.2}\]
For a given table \(\bar q\), write \(g_{\bar q}(s,a)\) for the expected TD target conditional on \(s_t=s\) and \(a_t=a\). The reward \(r(s,a)\) is the conditional mean of \(r_{t+1}\). Grouping the possible next states by their label gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_{\bar q}(s,a)
&=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal S}p(s'\given s,a)
                    \max_{b\in\mathcal A}\bar q(\phi(s'),b)\\
&=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{y\in\overline{\mathcal S}}
    p_\phi(y\given s,a)\max_{b\in\mathcal A}\bar q(y,b).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.3}\]
This is the expectation in the Q-learning Bellman equation with the continuation value taken from the shared table.

title: 5  State Abstraction
section: 5.2 When the abstract state is Markov
text:
5.2 When the abstract state is Markov
Let \(h_t\) be the history of observed labels, actions, and rewards through the current label \(x_t=x\), before taking action \(a_t\). Conditional on that history and the current action, the next label has distribution
\[
\Prob(x_{t+1}=y\given h_t,a_t=a)
=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_x}\Prob(s_t=s\given h_t,a_t=a)\,p_\phi(y\given s,a).
\tag{5.4}\]
This is the law of total probability. If \(p_\phi(y\given s,a)\) agrees across all \(s\in\mathcal S_x\) for every \(x,y,a\), we can take it outside the sum. The weights sum to one, and the result depends only on \(x\) and \(a\). The condition is also necessary for a single transition law valid from every full starting state. Start separately from any two states in the same group and take the same action. Their first-step distributions over labels must agree.
To preserve the one-step model, also require \(r(s,a)\) to agree within each group for every action. Then Equation 5.3 agrees within the group for every table \(\bar q\). The transition condition only compares the total probability of reaching each group. Within a destination group, the probabilities of reaching particular full states may differ. Li, Walsh, and Littman, Definition 3(1).

Under a fixed policy
The forecast in Equation 5.4 conditions on the current action. Under a fixed stationary policy \(\pi(a\given s)\), we can instead predict the next label before seeing the action. Chapter 2 averages over the action to get \(r_\pi(s)\) and \(p_\pi(s'\given s)\) (Definition 2.1). Applying Equation 5.2 to \(p_\pi\) gives the transition probability to label \(y\),
\[
\sum_{s'\in\mathcal S_y}p_\pi(s'\given s)
=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}\pi(a\given s)\,p_\phi(y\given s,a).
\]
For a single transition law under \(\pi\) valid from every starting state, this sum must agree across \(s\in\mathcal S_x\) for every \(x,y\). To preserve the expected reward under \(\pi\), check \(r_\pi(s)\) within each group as well. The policy averages can agree even when the probabilities differ for an individual action. If the policy uses only \(x\), agreement for each action also gives agreement after averaging over the policy.

title: 5  State Abstraction
text:
5.3 An MDP on abstract states
We can construct an MDP on the labels by choosing a distribution \(w_x(s)\) over the full states in each group \(\mathcal S_x\). Keep the same actions and discount factor, and define its reward and transition probability by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bar r(x,a)&=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_x} w_x(s)\,r(s,a),\\
\bar p(y\given x,a)&=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_x} w_x(s)\,p_\phi(y\given s,a).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.5}\]
The second expression averages probability distributions, so it defines a probability distribution for each \((x,a)\). Under the model conditions above, every term in each average agrees and the weights do not affect the result. In general the weights here are fixed by construction. The weights in Equation 5.4 describe which full state we occupy given the history and action, so they can change from one observation to the next. Li, Walsh, and Littman, Definition 1.
The Bellman optimality operator \(\bar T\) for the averaged MDP applies the right-hand side of the Q-learning Bellman equation to the current table. From Equation 5.5 and Equation 5.3,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\bar T\bar q)(x,a)
&=\bar r(x,a)+\gamma\sum_{y\in\overline{\mathcal S}}\bar p(y\given x,a)
                    \max_{b\in\mathcal A}\bar q(y,b)\\
&=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_x}w_x(s)\,g_{\bar q}(s,a).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.6}\]
The operator contracts by \(\gamma\). A change of at most \(\varepsilon\) in each table entry changes a maximum by at most \(\varepsilon\) and the discounted average by at most \(\gamma\varepsilon\). Its unique fixed point \(\bar q^*\) is the optimal action-value function of the averaged MDP.
If each sample for \((x,a)\) starts with a fresh draw \(s\) from \(w_x\) and then takes action \(a\) in the full MDP, its expected TD target is \((\bar T\bar q)(x,a)\). Use the per-entry step size conditions in Theorem 3.3. The step sizes on updates to each entry must be positive and at most one, with a divergent sum and a finite sum of squares. For this sampler, choose the step size after selecting \((x,a)\) and before drawing \(s\). The step size then cannot change the relative weight of different full states in the update. With infinitely many such samples for each pair, tabular Q-learning converges to \(\bar q^*\).
Along a trajectory, changing the behavior policy can change which full states supply updates to a shared entry. The expected TD target then averages Equation 5.3 with the conditional weights in Equation 5.4.

title: 5  State Abstraction
text:
5.4 Preserving values and decisions

Optimal action values
The full optimal action values \(q^*(s,a)\) fit in one table on the labels exactly when they agree within every group for each action. The model condition is sufficient. Start value iteration for the full Q-table at zero. If an iterate agrees within each group, its Bellman update is given by Equation 5.3 and also agrees under the model condition. The limit \(q^*\) has the same property.
Suppose \(q^*(s,a)\) agrees within each group, even though some transitions or expected rewards may differ. Define a candidate table by \(\bar q(\phi(s),a)=q^*(s,a)\). Substituting this table into Equation 5.3 gives \(g_{\bar q}(s,a)=q^*(s,a)\) by the full Bellman equation. Consequently every weighted average in Equation 5.6 returns the same entry \(\bar q(x,a)\). This table is the fixed point \(\bar q^*\) for any choice of weights.
The same equality explains why Q-learning can recover \(q^*\) without a fixed mix of full states. At the table representing \(q^*\), the expected TD error is zero conditional on each full pair \((s,a)\). For any other table \(\bar q\),
\[
\big|g_{\bar q}(s,a)-\bar q^*(\phi(s),a)\big|
\leq \gamma\|\bar q-\bar q^*\|_\infty .
\]
The contraction argument now applies at each full state before averaging. Suppose each full state-action pair is visited infinitely often and each step size is chosen before the new reward and next state. Under the same per-entry step size bounds and sums, the shared Q-table converges to the table representing \(q^*\). Li, Walsh, and Littman, Definition 3(3), Theorem 4(1).


An optimal policy
A policy \(\bar\pi(a\given x)\) on the labels acts in the full MDP by choosing actions with probabilities \(\pi(a\given s)=\bar\pi(a\given\phi(s))\). Such a policy can be optimal from every full state exactly when each group has an action that is optimal for all its members,
\[
\bigcap_{s\in\mathcal S_x}\argmax_{a\in\mathcal A}q^*(s,a)\ne\varnothing
\qquad\text{for every }x.
\tag{5.7}\]
An optimal policy must put its probability on maximizing actions, so its support at \(x\) must lie in the intersection. Conversely, choose an action from each intersection. The optimal state value \(v^*(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal A}q^*(s,a)\) then satisfies the Bellman equation of that policy, hence is its value. The condition requires a common maximizing action. Its value may vary across states in the group. Li, Walsh, and Littman, Definition 3(5).


When solving the averaged MDP gives an optimal policy
Suppose each group has both a common optimal action and a common optimal state value \(v^*(s)=\bar v(x)\) for \(s\in\mathcal S_x\). The return from taking action \(a\) in the averaged MDP and using \(\bar v\) for the continuation is
\[
\bar r(x,a)+\gamma\sum_{y\in\overline{\mathcal S}}\bar p(y\given x,a)\,\bar v(y)
=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_x}w_x(s)\,q^*(s,a)
\leq \bar v(x).
\tag{5.8}\]
A common optimal action attains equality, so \(\bar v\) solves the averaged Bellman equation. If every full state in the group has positive weight, an action attains equality only if it maximizes \(q^*(s,a)\) at every full state in the group. Thus a greedy policy from the averaged MDP is optimal in the full MDP. With those same sampling weights, Q-learning can learn this policy even when the values of suboptimal actions vary within a group. Changing the mix of samples can prevent those action values from converging. Li, Walsh, and Littman, Definition 3(4), Theorems 3 and 4(2).
If the common action has different values at different full states, the policy can still use the labels. The averaged Bellman equation replaces those different continuation values by a single value. This can reverse the ranking of actions that lead into the group. In that case both solving the averaged MDP and running Q-learning on samples with its fixed weights can yield a suboptimal policy. Li, Walsh, and Littman, Theorems 3–4 and Figure 1(b).

title: 5  State Abstraction
text:
5.5 The Krusell–Smith benchmark
Households save to insure against employment risk. Their saving determines next period’s aggregate capital and hence the prices they expect to face. The question is how well households can forecast those prices when they summarize the distribution of capital and employment with aggregate capital.

Household problem and equilibrium
In a population of mass one, each household holds capital \(k\geq 0\) and has employment status \(e\in\{0,1\}\). It supplies \(\ell\) units of labor if employed (\(e=1\)) and zero if unemployed (\(e=0\)). Aggregate productivity \(z\) moves between good and bad states according to a Markov chain. Write \(P(z',e'\given z,e)\) for the joint transition probability of next period’s productivity \(z'\) and employment \(e'\). Conditional on the aggregate transition, a law of large numbers applies to the employment shocks. The benchmark transition probabilities fix the employment share at each \(z\). Krusell and Smith (1998), §II.A.
Let \(\Gamma\) be the joint distribution of capital and employment. The household’s full state is \(s=(k,e,z,\Gamma)\). Assume aggregate capital \(K=\int k\,d\Gamma\) is positive and finite. Aggregate labor is \(L(z)=\ell\int e\,d\Gamma\). Since population mass is one, \(K\) is also mean household capital. With capital share \(\alpha\), aggregate output is \(Y=zK^\alpha L(z)^{1-\alpha}\). Competitive firms pay marginal products, so the wage per unit of labor \(w\) and rental rate of capital \(\rho\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
w(K,z) &= \frac{\partial Y}{\partial L} = (1-\alpha)z\left(\frac{K}{L(z)}\right)^\alpha,\\
\rho(K,z) &= \frac{\partial Y}{\partial K} = \alpha z\left(\frac{K}{L(z)}\right)^{\alpha-1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.9}\]
The household’s action \(a=k'\) chooses its capital for next period. Let \(c\) be consumption and \(\delta\) the depreciation rate. Labor income, capital income, and undepreciated capital fund consumption and saving. The budget and borrowing constraint are
\[
c+a=w(K,z)\ell e + \big(1-\delta+\rho(K,z)\big)k,
\qquad c>0,\quad a\geq 0.
\tag{5.10}\]
Households have flow utility \(\log c\) and common discount factor \(0<\gamma<1\). Under the benchmark calibration, next-period unemployment has positive probability from either employment status. Krusell and Smith (1998), §III.A.
Let \(H(\Gamma,z,z')\) denote the distribution law that a household takes as given. Its own saving has zero weight in the aggregate. Substituting consumption from Equation 5.10 gives the Bellman equation
\[
v(k,e,z,\Gamma)=
\max_{a}\left\{
  \log c+\gamma\,\E\!\left[v\big(a,e',z',H(\Gamma,z,z')\big)\given z,e\right]
\right\}.
\tag{5.11}\]
The maximum is over choices satisfying Equation 5.10. The expectation is over the joint shock transition, and the value at a state with zero resources is \(-\infty\). Krusell and Smith (1998), §II.B.
Write \(g(k,e,z,\Gamma)\) for the saving rule from Equation 5.11 and \(P(e'\given e,z,z')\) for the employment transition probability conditional on \(z'\). For a measurable set \(B\) of capital holdings, the mass entering \(B\) with employment status \(e'\) is
\[
\Gamma'(B\times\{e'\}) =
\int \mathbf{1}\{g(k,e,z,\Gamma)\in B\}\,
  P(e'\given e,z,z')\,d\Gamma(k,e).
\tag{5.12}\]
The indicator selects households that save an amount in \(B\). The conditional probability assigns their next employment status. This defines the distribution law \(H_g\) induced by \(g\). Summing over \(e'\) and taking the mean of next-period capital gives
\[
K'(\Gamma,z)=\int k'\,d\Gamma'=\int g(k,e,z,\Gamma)\,d\Gamma(k,e).
\tag{5.13}\]
Households choose \(k'\) before \(z'\) is realized, so current \(\Gamma\) and \(z\) determine \(K'\). Next period’s prices in Equation 5.9 use \(K'\) and \(z'\). Integrating Equation 5.10 yields \(C+K'=Y+(1-\delta)K\), where \(C=\int c\,d\Gamma\), since factor payments exhaust output. A recursive competitive equilibrium requires competitive prices, a saving rule that solves the household problem given \(H\), and consistency \(H=H_g\).


What the abstract state preserves
Replace \(\Gamma\) with mean household capital \(K\) to obtain the abstract state \(x=\phi(s)=(k,e,z,K)\). Capital and saving choices are continuous. The transition condition from the finite model requires the probability laws of the next abstract state to agree on every measurable set. Take two full states in the same group \(\mathcal S_x\) and fix the same feasible action \(a\) in both. Current prices agree because \(K\) and \(z\) agree and aggregate labor is fixed by \(z\). The budget set and current utility \(\log c\) at that action therefore agree.
The next abstract state is \((a,e',z',K'(\Gamma,z))\). The law of \((z',e')\) depends only on \((z,e)\), and the household’s action fixes its own next capital in both states. Since \(K'(\Gamma,z)\) is determined before the shocks arrive, the laws of the next abstract state agree exactly when the two distributions imply the same \(K'\) in Equation 5.13.
Suppose the saving rule is affine in individual capital, \(g(k,e,z,\Gamma)=b_e(z,K)+d(z,K)k\). The intercept \(b_e\) can depend on employment, and the slope \(d\) is common across employment states. Integrating gives
\[
K'(\Gamma,z)=d(z,K)K+
\sum_{e=0}^{1} b_e(z,K)\,\Gamma([0,\infty)\times\{e\}).
\]
Each employment share \(\Gamma([0,\infty)\times\{e\})\) depends only on \(z\), so the right-hand side depends only on \((z,K)\). With a nonlinear saving rule, two distributions with the same mean can place different masses where saving responds differently to capital. This can change \(K'\). In the benchmark simulation, most capital is held by households whose saving slopes are close to one another. The poorest households have lower slopes and hold little capital. Krusell and Smith (1998), §III.D and Figure 2.


Solving with aggregate capital
Let \(F_z(K)\) be the household’s forecast of next-period aggregate capital. Krusell and Smith use a log-linear rule with separate coefficients \(b_{0,z}\) and \(b_{1,z}\) for each productivity state.
\[
\log F_z(K)=b_{0,z}+b_{1,z}\log K.
\tag{5.14}\]

Guess the coefficients and solve the household problem with the same budget. In Equation 5.11, use the continuation value \(v_F(a,e',z',F_z(K))\) under the forecast. This gives the saving rule \(g_F(k,e,z,K)\).
Simulate a large panel of households along a productivity path. At each date, evaluate \(g_F\) at the panel’s current \(K_t\). Advance the joint distribution as in Equation 5.12 using the chosen capital and new employment of each household. In their finite panel, the authors adjusted simulated employment statuses to match the employment share implied by productivity in that quarter. The mean of the saving choices gives \(K_{t+1}\) for the next simulation step. Krusell and Smith (1998), Appendix A, p. 893.
After discarding the initial periods, regress \(\log K_{t+1}\) on a constant and \(\log K_t\) separately for each \(z_t\). Re-solve with the refitted coefficients and repeat until the fitted and conjectured coefficients agree to numerical tolerance.

At this fixed point, the forecast is the best fit in its class to the aggregate capital series generated by the saving rule it induces. Krusell and Smith (1998), §II.C.


Published forecast checks
Krusell and Smith compare one-quarter forecasts \(\log F_{z_t}(K_t)\) with \(\log K_{t+1}\), using \(K_t\) and \(K_{t+1}\) from the household simulation. They retain 10,000 quarters after discarding the first 1,000. In each productivity state, the share of variation in \(\log K_{t+1}\) explained by the regression is \(R^2=0.999998\). The standard deviation of the log forecast residual, expressed in percent, is \(0.0028\%\) in good times and \(0.0036\%\) in bad times. Krusell and Smith (1998), §§III.B–C.
Den Haan’s recursive check starts with a new productivity path and a common initial capital stock. Simulating the household distribution under the given saving rule yields the reference series \(K_t\). On the same productivity path, iterate the forecast on its own predicted capital.
\[
\widetilde K_0=K_0,\qquad
\widetilde K_{t+1}=F_{z_t}(\widetilde K_t).
\tag{5.15}\]
Compare \(\log\widetilde K_t\) with \(\log K_t\) at each horizon \(t\). The maximum absolute gap shows how far the paths diverge. den Haan (2010), §2.4.
In a separate illustration, den Haan fits a forecast rule to 10,000 observations from a simulation of the Krusell–Smith model using Young’s household policies. One altered rule has a one-step \(R^2\) of \(0.9999\) on those observations. The standard deviation of \(\log K\) implied by the fitted rule is close to that in the household simulation and about \(14\%\) higher than that implied by the altered rule. den Haan (2010), Table 1.
These checks assess forecasts against aggregates from a given household policy. Accuracy relative to the full-state equilibrium also depends on how household choices change when households forecast the full distribution.


Estimating the discount factor
Vary the common discount factor \(0<\gamma<1\) and hold the remaining calibration fixed. For each candidate, solve the full-state equilibrium with \(s\). With the abstract state \(x\), solve the household problem and refit \(F_z\) to convergence as above. Start all simulations from the same distribution, with positive capital for every household, a finite mean, and the employment share implied by initial productivity. Use the same productivity path in all simulations and the same employment shock draws in household panels.
After discarding the same initial quarters, keep the next \(T\) quarters from each simulation. Compute \(K_t\) from simulated saving choices using Equation 5.13 and use quarterly output \(Y_t=z_tK_t^\alpha L(z_t)^{1-\alpha}\). For each representation \(j\in\{\mathrm{full},\mathrm{abstract}\}\), average the capital-output ratio and the zero-capital share \(p_{0,t}\).
\[
p_{0,t}=\int \mathbf{1}\{k=0\}\,d\Gamma_t(k,e),\qquad
m_j(\gamma)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T
\begin{pmatrix}K_t/Y_t\\ p_{0,t}\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{5.16}\]
The share uses the full simulated \(\Gamma_t\) even when households forecast with \(x\). Across arbitrary distributions, the same mean \(K_t\) is consistent with different zero-capital shares because higher holdings among households with positive capital can offset a larger mass at zero.
Under either representation, choosing \(a=0\) leaves the household with zero resources if it is unemployed next quarter, by Equation 5.10. That event has positive probability from either current employment status, so the action gives expected lifetime utility \(-\infty\). Starting with positive resources, consider saving a fixed fraction of current resources each quarter, with the fraction strictly between zero and one. Because \(1-\delta>0\), consumption along this plan is bounded below by a positive geometric sequence. For \(0<\gamma<1\), discounted log utility along that plan is bounded below. An optimal choice therefore has strictly positive next-period capital \(k'\). Krusell and Smith (1998), §III.A.
Write \(g_t(k,e)\) for either saving rule evaluated at the current aggregate state. Summing Equation 5.12 over \(e'\) for \(B=\{0\}\) gives a zero share from the first transition onward.
\[
p_{0,t+1}=\int \mathbf{1}\{g_t(k,e)=0\}\,d\Gamma_t(k,e)=0.
\tag{5.17}\]
Let \(\widehat m_1\) and \(\widehat m_2\) be the observed targets, calculated as time averages of the same two quarterly measures in Equation 5.16. For each \(j\), minimize the criterion on a common grid of \(\gamma\) values using these targets and the same positive weights \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\).
\[
J_j(\gamma)=\omega_1\big[m_{j,1}(\gamma)-\widehat m_1\big]^2
           +\omega_2\big[m_{j,2}(\gamma)-\widehat m_2\big]^2.
\tag{5.18}\]
The zero-capital share is a diagnostic of fit with a constant contribution \(\omega_2\widehat m_2^2\) in both representations. Compare changes in \(m_{j,1}(\gamma)\) between nearby candidates with simulation error and solution error. Use longer simulations and finer solution grids to gauge those errors. Compare the minimizing candidates across representations and check whether separated candidates fit equally well.

TipReading a value symbol



Value symbols distinguish the following independent choices.

What is being valued: a state (\(v\)) or a state-action pair (\(q\)).
Under which policy: a given \(\pi\) (subscript \(\pi\), an evaluation object) or the best one (superscript \(*\), an optimality object).
Estimate or truth: no decoration is the true value; a time subscript \(v_{t},q_{t}\) is the running estimate; a hat \(\hat{v},\hat{q}\) is a parameterized approximation.
